title: Wedding Wine and a Disrupted Temple
overview: Jesus turns water into wine at a village wedding, then drives traders out of the Jerusalem temple and hints at his own death and rising.

parts.label: The wine runs out (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Village weddings could last days, and running out of wine would have embarrassed the hosts in front of everyone. Calling his mother "woman" was not rude then, and his "hour" is John's term for the time of his death and glory, so he seems to mean he acts on his own timing, not that he refuses to help.

parts.label: Water becomes wine (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: The six large stone jars held water for ritual washing, a way of staying religiously clean, and Jesus fills them with far more fine wine than the party could use. John calls this the first "sign," an act pointing beyond itself to who Jesus is, and many readers see washing water turned into festive wine as a picture of something new and generous arriving.

parts.label: A short stay nearby (v. 12)
parts.note: Jesus goes down to Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee that became a base for his work. Christians have long differed on whether the brothers mentioned here were later sons of Mary or close relatives such as cousins.

parts.label: Clearing the temple courts (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: At Passover, pilgrims needed animals to sacrifice and had to change their coins into the money accepted for temple payments, so traders worked in the outer courts. Jesus drives them out for turning his "Father's house" into a market, and the disciples recall a line from Psalm 69 about burning devotion to God's house.

parts.label: Destroy this temple (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: The religious leaders demand proof of his right to do this, and his reply sounds like a claim about the building, which King Herod's rebuilding had kept under construction for 46 years. John says he meant his own body, which the disciples understood only after the resurrection, and Christians read it as Jesus becoming the true place where people meet God.

parts.label: Faith built on wonders (vv. 23-25)
parts.note: Many in Jerusalem believed because they saw miracles, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them, since he knew what people are like. John seems to suggest that belief resting only on spectacle can be shallow, a theme he returns to later.

disagreement: Christians differ on how much symbolism to read into the wine sign, some seeing it mainly as a picture of old religious rituals giving way to something new, others as a simpler display of kindness and abundance.
think: When someone does something impressive, what makes you trust them, and what makes you hold back?
